'''''Stellaria neglecta''''', '''greater chickweed''', is an [[annual plant|annual]] to short-lived [[herbaceous]] [[perennial]] [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Caryophyllaceae]]. It is native to [[Europe]] and [[Asia]], where it grows in hedges and woodland margins on neutral to slightly acid, damp soils, and is widespread but rarely abundant. It has been introduced to North America, where it has been spreading in recent decades.

==Description==
A sprawling annual (to short-lived perennial) with weak branching stems that are usually [[decumbent]] at the base, ascending [[distally]] to around {{Convert abbreviated|80-90|cm}}, often supported by other plants. The stems are cylindrical and [[Glabrousness|glabrous]] except for a single line of hairs that runs lengthways, changing sides at each node. Other parts of the plant are usually entirely glabrous. The leaves are arranged in opposite pairs, the lower ones having long (2−5 cm), narrowly winged [[Petiole (botany)|stalks]] and a broadly oval-triangular blade about 3 cm long by 1.5 cm wide. The upper leaves are [[Sessility (botany)|sessile]] or only very shortly [[Petiole (botany)|petiolate]], slightly larger and more oval. The leaves have one strong central vein along the midrib and about 5 lateral veins on each side.<ref name="Clapham">{{cite book |last1=Clapham |first1=Arthur Roy |author-link1=Arthur Roy Clapham |last2=Tutin |first2=Thomas Gaskell |author-link2= Tom Tutin|last3=Warburg |first3=E F |author-link3= E. F. Warburg |title=Flora of the British Isles |edition=2nd |year=1962 |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] |isbn=0-521-26962-8}}</ref><ref name=Poland>{{cite book |last1=Poland |first1=John |last2=Clement |first2=Eric |title=The Vegetative Key to the British Flora |date=2009 |publisher=John Poland |location=Southampton |isbn=978-0-9560144-0-5}}</ref><ref name="efloras">{{cite book | url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=242000911 | title=Flora of North America: north of Mexico | publisher=[[Oxford University Press]] | pages=110 }}</ref>
[[File:Stellaria neglecta upper leaves.jpg|thumb|The upper leaves are sessile and somewhat rectangular in outline.]]

The flowers are borne singly in the uppermost leaf axils on slender 2−3 cm stalks, initially spreading and reflexed, later erect. Each flower has five [[Sepal|sepals]], 5−6.5 mm long, [[lanceolate]], glabrous or rarely pubescent, with an acute apex. There are also five white petals which are divided almost to the base, giving the impression that there are ten. The petals are usually about the same length as the sepals or just slightly shorter, the whole flower being about 10 mm in diameter. There are 8−10 [[Stamen|stamens]] with reddish anthers, and three styles.<ref name="Whitehead">{{cite journal |doi=10.1111/j.1469-8137.1967.tb05444.x |last=Whitehead |first=F. H. |author2=R. P. Sinha  |date=October 1967 |title=Taxonomy and Taximetrics of ''Stellaria media'' (L.) Vill., ''S. neglecta'' Weihe and ''S. pallida'' (Dumort.) Pire |journal=New Phytologist |publisher=[[Blackwell Publishing]] |volume=66 |issue=4 |pages=769–784 |jstor=2430464|doi-access= }}</ref><ref name="Clapham" /><ref name="efloras" /><ref name=Stace>{{cite book |last1=Stace |first1=C.A. |title=New Flora of the British Isles |date=2019 |location=Suffolk |isbn=978-1-5272-2630-2}}</ref>
[[File:Stellaria neglecta W.jpg|thumb|right |The flowers have ten stamens, although sometimes only the filaments remain.]]

It flowers between April and July in Northern Europe.<ref name="Clapham" /> The stems can remain alive and produce [[Tiller (botany)|tillers]] which overwinter and flower the following year.<ref name="Whitehead" /> Seeds are [[tubercle|tuberculate]], dark reddish-brown, 1.3−1.7 mm in diameter.<ref name="Clapham" /> The [[Tubercle|tubercles]] are conical, with an acute apex.<ref name="efloras" />

==Taxonomy==
This species was first published by [[Alexandre Louis Simon Lejeune]] in 1825 as ''Alsine neglecta'', which is therefore the basionym. It was then (the same year) moved to the genus ''Stellaria'' <small>L.</small> by [[Carl Ernst August Weihe]] and this name is accepted to this day.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Plants of the World Online |title=Stellaria neglecta (Lej.) Weihe |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:159358-1 |access-date=11 April 2023}}</ref> Over the years many synonyms have been coined, such as ''Alsine decandra'' <small>Schur</small> (in 1866), ''Stellaria media'' var. ''decandra'' <small>Fenzl</small> (in 1842) and ''Stellaria decandra'' <small>Schur ex Prodan</small> (in 1953). A full list is given by the Synonymic Checklists of the Vascular Plants of the World.<ref name=GBIF>{{cite web |last1=Global Biodiversity Information Facility |title=Stellaria neglecta (Lej.) Weihe |url=https://www.gbif.org/species/6363436 |access-date=11 April 2023}}</ref>

Numerous subspecies, varieties and forms have been named, but none is currently accepted<ref name="GBIF" /> and it is not known to hybridise with any other species.<ref name=hybrids>{{cite book |last1=Stace |first1=C.A. |last2=Preston |first2=C.D. |last3=Pearman |first3=D.A. |title=Hybrid Flora of the British Isles |date=2015 |publisher=Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland |location=Bristol |isbn=978-0-901158-48-2}}</ref>

Its chromosome number is 2n = 22.<ref name="Stace" />

The scientific name ''Stellaria'' means "like a star" in reference to the flowers, and ''neglecta'' is in acknowledgement that it was long overlooked,<ref name=Stearn>{{cite book |last1=Stearn |first1=William T. |title=Botanical Latin: History, Grammar, Syntax, Terminology and Vocabulary |date=1980 |publisher=David & Charles |location=Newton Abbot |isbn=0-7153-5645-3}}</ref> as it often still is to this day.<ref name=Atlas>{{cite book |last1=Preston |first1=C.D. |last2=Pearman |first2=D.A. |last3=Dines |first3=T.D. |title=New Atlas of the British and Irish Flora |date=2002 |publisher=Oxford University Press |location=Oxford}}</ref>

==Identification==
Three species of chickweed have a single line of hairs down the stem. There are various features which can be used to separate them: ''[[Stellaria apetala]]'' usually has 1–3 [[stamen]]s and no white petals; ''[[Stellaria media|S. media]]'' has 3–8 stamens and white petals up to 3 mm long; whereas ''S. neglecta'' usually has 10 stamens and petals up to 4 mm. As the anthers often fall off, it is best to count the filaments.<ref name="Stace" /><ref name=Rose>{{cite book |last1=Rose |first1=Francis |title=The Wild Flower Key |date=2006 |publisher=Frederick Warne |location=London|isbn=978-0-7232-5175-0}}</ref>

In the absence of flowers, the size of the plants (up to 10 cm; 25 cm; 100 cm) is a useful character, as are the leaves (up to 7 mm; 25 mm; 50 mm respectively), which also look rather different on the various species.<ref name="Poland" />

{{Plain image with caption|Leaves of three species of chickweed.jpg|A leaf of ''Stellaria apetala'' (left), ''S. media'' (middle) and ''S. neglecta'' (right). Not to scale.|600px|centre}}

==Distribution and status==
Greater chickweed is widely distributed throughout Europe and southern Asia as far east as Japan.<ref name="GBIF" /><ref>{{cite web | url=http://luirig.altervista.org/schedeit2/pz/stellaria_neglecta.htm | title=Stellaria neglecta Weihe | access-date=2010-08-13}}</ref> In Great Britain, it is most common in the south and west.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.searchnbn.net/gridMap/gridMapLarge.jsp#topOfMap | title=Grid map of records on the Gateway for Stellaria neglecta (Greater Chickweed) | publisher=National Biodiversity Network | year=2010 | access-date=2010-08-13}}</ref> In North America, it was formerly rare, but it has spread rapidly in recent decades and is now considered a weed in a number of states, from [[Maryland]] to [[California]].<ref name="efloras" />

The international status of greater chickweed has not been evaluated,<ref>{{cite web |last1=European Nature Information System |title=Stellaria neglecta Weihe |url=https://eunis.eea.europa.eu/species/166759 |access-date=12 April 2023}}</ref> but in Britain it is classified as "Least Concern" on the grounds that it is still widespread, albeit declining.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Cheffings |first1=C.M. | last2=Farrell |first2=L. |title=The Vascular Plant Red Data List for Great Britain |date=2005 |publisher=Joint Nature Conservation Committee |location=Peterborough}}</ref><ref name=Atlas>{{cite book |last1=Preston |first1=C.D. |last2=Pearman |first2=D.A. |last3=Dines |first3=T.D. |title=New Atlas of the British and Irish Flora |date=2002 |publisher=Oxford University Press |location=Oxford}}</ref> In France it is similarly not threatened except in the Alsace region, where it is considered to be vulnerable.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Inventaire National du Patrimoine Naturel |title=Stellaria neglecta Weihe, 1825 |url=https://inpn.mnhn.fr/espece/cd_nom/125019 |access-date=12 April 2023}}</ref>

==Habitat and ecology==
Greater chickweed grows in lightly shaded situations on slightly damp, base-rich and moderately fertile soils. Its [[Indicator value|Ellenberg values]] in Britain are L = 6, F = 7, R = 6, N = 7, and S = 0.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Hill|first1=M.O.|last2=Mountford|first2=J.O.|last3=Roy|first3=D.B.|last4=Bunce|first4=R.G.H.|title=Ellenberg's indicator values for British plants. ECOFACT Volume 2. Technical Annex|date=1999|publisher=Institute of Terrestrial Ecology|isbn=1870393481|url=http://nora.nerc.ac.uk/6411/1/ECOFACT2a.pdf|accessdate=29 May 2017}}</ref> It is often found in old hedges and on the margins and paths of ancient deciduous woodland, where it is generally sparsely distributed and tends to occur in small patches.<ref name=Crawley>{{cite book |last1=Crawley |first1=M.J. |title=The Flora of Berkshire |date=2005 |publisher=Brambleby Books |location=Harpenden |isbn=0-9543347-4-4}}</ref><ref name=Lockton>{{cite book |last1=Lockton |first1=Alex |last2=Whild |first2=Sarah |title=The Flora and Vegetation of Shropshire |date=2015 |publisher=Shropshire Botanical Society |location=Montford Bridge |url=https://archive.org/details/flora-and-vegetation-of-shropshire-2015}}</ref>

In terms of the [[British National Vegetation Classification]] it is recorded in MG1 [[Arrhenatherum elatius|false oatgrass]] swards on woodland edges, W6 [[Salix × fragilis|crack willow]] woodland by rivers, in W10 [[Quercus robur|oak]] woodland and W24 [[Rubus fruticosus|bramble]] scrub in hedges.<ref name="Lockton" /> Because it is quite scarce and declining, and largely restricted to old hedges and woods, it is considered an [[axiophyte]] in some counties.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland |title=Kent |url=https://bsbi.org/kent |access-date=12 April 2023}}</ref><ref name="Lockton" />

It is a lowland plant, reaching its altitudinal limit of {{Convert abbreviated|345|m}} in Britain on Stapeley Hill in Shropshire.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Plant Atlas 2020 |title=Greater Chickweed, Stellaria neglecta Weihe |url=https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.p7m |access-date=13 April 2023}}</ref>

Presumably because it is such a little-known plant, there are no recorded instances of insect associations with this species in Britain.<ref name=PIDB>{{cite web |last1=Biological Records Centre |title=Insects and their food plants |url=http://dbif.brc.ac.uk/ |access-date=30 April 2022}}</ref> There are also no known galls, rusts or smuts.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Redfern |first1=Margaret |last2=Shirley |first2=Peter |title=British Plant Galls |journal=Field Studies |date=2002 |volume=10 |pages=207–531}}</ref>
